A 21-year-old woman presented with lifelong uncorrectable visual acuity and color vision impairment. There was no consanguinity in her family. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. She had myopia (–6.0 diopters) and intraocular pressures of 17 mmHg bilaterally. Fundus examination showed slight enlargement of the cup-to-disc ratio in both eyes. Visual field testing revealed a central scotoma in both eyes. Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging demonstrated symmetric hypoautofluorescent lesions with hyperautofluorescent borders in the central macula bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed thinning of the outer nuclear layer in the fovea, partial preservation of the ellipsoid zone, and a normal retinal nerve fiber layer. Full-field electroretinography (ff-ERG) revealed normal scotopic responses but attenuated photopic responses and 30-Hz flicker responses with delayed implicit times in both eyes.

Her 54-year-old father reported over 10 years of progressive blurred central vision and color vision defects. He had myopia (–3.0 diopters) and no other relevant family history. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in both eyes. Intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg in the right eye and 16 mmHg in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed macular atrophy and lesions bilaterally. FAF imaging showed an outer ring of increased autofluorescence with central hypoautofluorescence in the macula of both eyes. OCT demonstrated loss of the ellipsoid zone and collapse of the outer nuclear layer in the central macula bilaterally. ff-ERG showed delayed implicit times in the dark-adapted 0.01 ERG, an electronegative waveform in the dark-adapted 3.0 ERG, and non-recordable photopic and 30-Hz flicker responses in both eyes.

A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use was transferred for evaluation of altered mental status. He was found minimally responsive and arrived febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10), requiring intubation for airway protection. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage. Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema, scattered small foci of restricted diffusion, and subtle punctate blooming on susceptibility-weighted images; there was no enhancement after gadolinium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³ (57% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 81 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL (serum 121 mg/dL); Gram stain was negative. Initial CSF studies were negative for acid-fast bacilli, herpes simplex virus PCR, and fungi. Empirical IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were begun; his leukocytosis improved but fever persisted. 

On hospital day 5 he became more obtunded. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³ (60% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 123 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (serum 105 mg/dL), and no red cells. Rickettsial studies, multiple viral cultures including John Cunningham virus PCR, quantiferon gold, and protozoal investigations were also negative. Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement. 

Because the etiology remained unclear and the patient was deteriorating, a brain biopsy was planned.

An 82-year-old man with epithelioid pleural mesothelioma (cT1N0M0) was treated with ipilimumab and nivolumab. After eight courses, follow-up chest CT showed new bilateral infiltrative shadows. Serologic testing for anti–nuclear antigen, anti–aminoacyl–tRNA synthetase, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, anti-Sjögren’s-syndrome-related antigen A and B, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antigen antibodies were all negative. He had no history of antigen exposure. Immunotherapy was discontinued. He received lascufloxacin and then tazobactam/ceftolozane without improvement; oxygen requirement increased to 2 L/min. Based on the clinical picture and imaging, grade 3 ICI-induced pneumonitis was suspected. He underwent methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days followed by prednisolone 60 mg/day for 8 days, but chest radiographs remained unchanged and oxygen needs rose to 4 L/min. A second course of methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days produced no clinical improvement. One week later, bronchoscopy showed no airway secretions. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 29% neutrophils, 58% lymphocytes, 13% macrophages, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.33. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy, and cultures of bronchoscopy specimens were negative. Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with steroid-refractory ICI-induced pneumonitis.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by early satiety and urinary urgency. She denied pain, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Her menstrual cycles were normal, and her mother had a history of ovarian cysts. On examination, the abdomen was distended with dull percussion notes but without tenderness or guarding.

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a cyst measuring 16 × 24 cm that compressed adjacent abdominal organs. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a large midline intraperitoneal cyst, 30 × 25.6 × 16.8 cm in size, extending from the liver to the pelvis and involving the uterus and ovaries. The lesion had a fluid density of 20 Hounsfield units and demonstrated no calcifications, soft-tissue components, or enhancing septations, suggesting a benign etiology.

Laboratory studies, including α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, and cancer antigen 125, were all within normal limits; the Risk of Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA) score was 4.1 %. Serological testing for Echinococcus granulosus was negative. A giant intra-abdominal cyst was diagnosed preoperatively, and laparoscopic cyst aspiration with exploration under general anesthesia was planned.
